planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after soil has thoroughly warmed past last frost; Densuke originates from a limited cooperative harvest in Toma, Hokkaido, Japan, where its solid black rind and short cool-summer growing window made it a prized specialty melon.

directions: Sow 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil after all danger of frost has passed, spacing vines 3-6 feet apart in rows with ample room to sprawl. Densuke is distinguished from typical striped watermelons by a rind that ripens to an almost uniform matte black rather than developing stripes, enclosing crisp, sweet red flesh; the fruit was originally developed and marketed by a small growers' cooperative in Toma, Hokkaido, where the cooler northern Japanese summers and volcanic soil were credited with its intense sweetness. Give plants full sun and consistent moisture through fruit set, then ease off watering as melons near maturity to concentrate sugars. Harvest by checking the dulling of the ground spot and the drying of the tendril nearest the fruit stem, since the solid dark rind makes the classic thump test and stripe patterns unreliable ripeness cues.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after soil has thoroughly warmed, giving each vine a generous hill with heavily amended soil since this hybrid is bred purely for enormous fruit size, routinely exceeding 100 lbs and holding several giant-watermelon world records.

directions: Sow 1 inch deep in a heavily amended hill after last frost, allowing at least 8-10 feet in every direction per vine since this variety produces exceptionally long, vigorous runners. Carolina Cross #183 is an oblong striped hybrid bred specifically for maximum fruit size rather than eating quality, and it has been the variety of choice for generations of giant-watermelon growers at county fairs and record competitions, with individual fruits commonly reaching 100-200 lbs and record specimens well over 200 lbs. To grow oversized fruit, limit each vine to one or two developing melons, feed heavily throughout the season, and water deeply and consistently since the huge fruit places large demands on the root system. Flesh is red and reasonably sweet, but the plant's primary appeal is spectacle and competition rather than refined flavor.

common_name: Top Mark Cantaloupe (Classic Western Shipping Melon)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills once soil is thoroughly warm; Top Mark was bred by the Dessert Seed Company of El Centro, California as a firm-fleshed Western shipping cantaloupe and remains popular with home gardeners for its reliable disease tolerance and classic flavor.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills of two to three plants in full sun once soil has warmed well past last frost, thinning to the strongest seedling per hill. Top Mark produces slightly oblong, well-netted, 3-4 lb fruits with thick, firm, sweet salmon-colored flesh, and was long grown as a standard commercial shipping melon in California's Imperial Valley thanks to good tolerance of powdery and downy mildew. Keep soil evenly moist through vine growth and fruit set, then reduce watering as melons approach maturity to concentrate sweetness. Harvest at full slip, when the stem separates cleanly from the fruit with light pressure and the blossom end yields slightly to thumb pressure.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills once soil is thoroughly warm; PMR 45 was released in 1937 as the first cantaloupe bred for resistance to powdery mildew race 1 after the disease devastated California's Imperial Valley melon crop in the 1920s, and it remains foundational breeding stock for mildew-resistant melons today.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun after soil has warmed well past last frost, spacing hills 24-36 inches apart in rows several feet apart. PMR 45 produces medium-sized, well-netted, oval fruits with thick, sweet orange flesh, and was a landmark release in melon breeding as the first commercial cantaloupe bred specifically for resistance to powdery mildew, a disease that had caused catastrophic losses in California melon fields during the 1920s. Its resistance genes have since been used extensively by breeders to create many modern mildew-resistant melon hybrids, making it a historically significant variety as well as a solid, productive open-pollinated choice for home gardens. Water consistently through vine growth and fruit development, then taper off as melons approach maturity, and harvest at full slip when the stem separates cleanly from the fruit.
sources: UC Riverside Department of Plant Pathology
Cucurbit Breeding, North Carolina State University

planting.note: Direct sow in hills once soil is thoroughly warm; Emerald Gem arose as a chance seedling in a Michigan garden, was purchased and introduced by W. Atlee Burpee in 1886, and quickly became one of the most popular American muskmelons of the late 19th century for its rich, spicy-sweet flavor.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun after last frost, thinning to the strongest two or three plants per hill. Emerald Gem produces small, globe-shaped, deeply ribbed fruits with smooth, dark emerald-green skin that conceals thick, richly flavored, pale orange flesh often described as having a distinctive spicy sweetness beyond typical cantaloupe. Discovered as a chance seedling in the Michigan garden of William G. Voorhees, it was purchased and introduced commercially by W. Atlee Burpee in 1886 and quickly became a benchmark variety praised for combining fine flavor with dependable, uniform type. Because the fruit is compact and matures relatively quickly for a melon, it suits shorter-season gardens; keep soil evenly moist through fruit set and harvest at full slip, when the stem releases cleanly from the vine.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after soil has thoroughly warmed; Faerie was bred by Known-You Seed Company and named a 2012 All-America Selections winner for its creamy yellow, thin-striped rind, sweet pink-red flesh, and unusually compact vines that suit smaller gardens.

directions: Sow 1 inch deep in warm, well-drained soil after last frost, or start indoors 2-3 weeks earlier for a head start in cooler climates; vines are notably more restrained than most watermelons, spreading to roughly 10-11 feet rather than sprawling widely. Faerie was bred by Taiwan's Known-You Seed Company and named a 2012 All-America Selections winner for its distinctive creamy yellow rind marked with thin light stripes, enclosing crisp, high-sugar pink-red flesh, and for producing a heavy set of personal-size, 4-6 lb oval fruit on a comparatively space-efficient plant. Keep soil consistently moist through flowering and fruit set, then ease back as melons near maturity. Harvest by watching the ground spot shift from white to creamy yellow and the nearby tendril dry and brown, since the pale rind makes color-based ripeness cues less obvious than on dark-skinned watermelons.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant after soil has thoroughly warmed; Little Darling is a compact hybrid bred to deliver classic dark-rind, red-fleshed watermelon flavor and high sugar content on vines that take up notably less garden space than standard icebox types.

directions: Sow 1 inch deep in warm soil after last frost, spacing plants 2-3 feet apart since vines run only about 4-5 feet, considerably shorter than traditional watermelon varieties. Little Darling produces oblong, dark-striped fruits around 5 by 8 inches and 5-7 lbs, with crisp, sweet red flesh rating around 12 on the Brix sugar scale, making it a good choice for gardeners who want full-flavored, classic watermelon character without the space demands of large-vine heirlooms. Water deeply and consistently through flowering and fruit set, then reduce watering as fruit nears maturity to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip and by checking that the tendril nearest the fruit has dried and browned, since the compact plant can otherwise make ripeness easy to misjudge.

planting.note: Direct sow in hills once soil is thoroughly warm; Golden Jenny was selected from the historic Jenny Lind muskmelon line and produces small, round, golden-skinned fruit with sweet orange flesh on a plant well suited to compact gardens and short growing seasons.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun after last frost, thinning to the strongest two or three seedlings per hill; the compact vines and small fruit size make this a good candidate for raised beds or smaller vegetable plots. Golden Jenny produces round, one to two pound fruits with smooth golden-yellow skin and juicy, aromatic, orange-gold flesh, and was developed from the classic 19th-century Jenny Lind muskmelon, retaining that heirloom's sweetness and old-fashioned melon aroma in a smaller, quicker-maturing package. Keep soil evenly moist through vine growth and fruit set, then let it dry slightly as fruit nears ripeness to concentrate sugars. Harvest at full slip, when the stem separates cleanly from the vine with light pressure and the fruit releases a strong, sweet fragrance at the blossom end.

common_name: Schoon's Hard Shell Melon (Heirloom Shipping Cantaloupe)

planting.note: Direct sow in hills once soil is thoroughly warm; Schoon's Hard Shell is a heirloom muskmelon long prized for its exceptionally tough, durable rind that let it stand up to shipping and field handling far better than most old melon varieties, while still ripening to richly flavored salmon flesh.

directions: Sow seeds 1 inch deep in hills in full sun after soil has warmed well past last frost, allowing ample room for the vigorous vines to sprawl. Schoon's Hard Shell is a long-season heirloom muskmelon producing large, oval, heavily netted fruits, 7-8 inches long and 5-8 lbs, encased in an unusually thick, tough rind that made it an outstanding shipper and field-stander in an era before refrigerated transport, while the thick red-salmon flesh ripens to an intensely sweet, richly aromatic flavor. Because it is slow to mature relative to modern hybrids, gardeners in shorter-season regions may want to start it a bit earlier or choose a warm, sheltered planting site. Keep soil consistently moist through vine growth and fruit development, then reduce watering as melons approach maturity, and harvest at full slip when the stem separates cleanly from the fruit.
